summary: This review examines cryoelectronics integration for scaling superconducting fault-tolerant quantum computers (FTQCs), addressing how to move classical control and readout electronics from room-temperature racks into cryogenic stages to reduce wiring overhead and thermal load. Using an RSA-2048 benchmark ($\sim 9 \times 10^5$ physical qubits), the authors present a first-order power-budget framework connecting per-qubit dissipation, effective throughput $F$, and stage-wise cooling constraints across cryo-CMOS at 4 K and superconducting digital logic (SFQ/AQFP) at mK stages.
motivation: Scaling superconducting quantum computers toward $10^5$–$10^6$ physical qubits makes the conventional room-temperature rack approach infeasible due to prohibitive wiring density, thermal load, and cable count; cryogenic electronics can substantially reduce this burden by placing selected functions deeper in the dilution refrigerator.
method: The paper surveys representative control/readout architectures, compares cryo-CMOS (reported $\sim 2$–$23$ mW per qubit), SFQ pulse drivers ($\sim 1.6$ µW per qubit), and AQFP logic ($\sim 81.8$ pW per qubit), and uses $P_{\mathrm{fridge}}(T) = F \cdot N_{\mathrm{phys,fridge}} \cdot P_{\mathrm{phys}}(T)$ to relate per-physical-qubit dissipation to available cooling power at 4 K ($\sim$ few W) and 10–20 mK ($\sim 10$–$300$ µW).
result: At 10 mK, only ultra-low-power functions like AQFP are viable; at 4 K, cryo-CMOS and SFQ are feasible depending on throughput and multiplexing constraints; practical FTQCs require heterogeneous functional partitioning across room-temperature electronics, 4 K cryo-CMOS/SFQ, and mK AQFP to simultaneously satisfy bandwidth, latency, heat load, and qubit-compatibility constraints.
